title: Security review with Calder Water Authority
scratchpad:
notify 48h from confirmation, NOT 72 (old template)
pen test = Larkspire this yr, Ormsby Kade was 2 yrs ago
no dedicated instance -> residency addendum
Elena: revised questionnaire to Beatrix Wed 14th
segments: Okay, I think everyone's here. Graham, Beatrix, thanks for making the time. I know a security questionnaire review isn't anyone's favourite way to spend an afternoon.
Ha, it's literally my job, so I don't mind at all. Beatrix is joining because half of the flagged questions are really records questions, not security ones.
Hi everyone. Yes, I look after records management and compliance, so retention and anything touching public records requests ends up on my desk sooner or later.
Great to meet you properly, Beatrix. On our side, Odette runs infrastructure and security, and she wrote most of the technical answers you've been reading.
Hello. Fair warning, I wrote some of those answers quite late at night, so if anything reads oddly, please push on it.
So what I'd suggest is we go through the questions you flagged in order, and we capture anything we need to fix in writing afterwards.
That works for me. We flagged about thirty out of the hundred and forty. Most are clarifications, and a handful are things our auditors will definitely ask about.
And just so I have the context right, the questionnaire feeds into your vendor approval, and only then can the contract move forward?
Right. Nothing gets signed until security and records both sign off. And with the commission audit coming up, I'm being extra careful this year.
Understood. Can I ask about the audit for a second, just so we know what we're actually preparing for?
Sure. The regional utilities commission does a cyber review of every water authority. Ours was supposed to be early in the new year, sometime in January.
They look at our vendors too, especially anyone holding customer data or touching field operations. So you're in scope, I'm afraid.
That's fine, we expected it. Is there anything on the operational side we should know? I want to be sure we're nowhere near your control systems.
No, and that's actually question twelve. Quillmark only sees work orders, crew schedules and customer addresses. Nothing connects to our treatment plant controls.
Good. Then I'd like to confirm in writing that there's no integration with operational technology at all, and none planned on our side.
Can we start with retention? That's the section I flagged most heavily, and I suspect it's where our policies and your defaults don't quite line up.
Of course. Odette, do you want to describe what we actually store for them, before we get into how long?
Sure. We store work orders, the service addresses on those jobs, crew assignments, photos technicians take on site, and location breadcrumbs from the app while a shift is active.
And how long do you keep each of those? That's really the heart of most of my questions.
Work orders and photos are kept for as long as the contract is active. Location breadcrumbs are kept on a rolling ninety days, then purged automatically.
Ninety days for location is fine, though honestly we'd prefer less. Our crews' union asked about tracking last year, so less history is better for everyone.
We can shorten it per customer. Thirty days is the shortest we'd recommend, because dispatch uses that history to settle disputes about arrival times.
Let me take thirty days back to the union rep before we commit to anything. What happens to all of it when the contract ends?
When the contract ends you get a full export, and then we delete everything within ninety days. That's the standard language in our agreement.
Our records schedule says work orders have to be kept for seven years, but that's our obligation, not yours, as long as we get a complete export.
Exactly. The export includes the photos and the full job history as files you can keep in your own records system. We just shouldn't become your archive.
Agreed, I really don't want you as our archive. I'll want written confirmation when the deletion is done though, signed by someone on your side.
We do that already. You'd get a deletion letter from Odette's team once the purge completes, and it covers the backups as well.
Okay, that section's fine then. Next is access. We'd want single sign-on for everyone, including crews in the field, not only the dispatchers.
SSO is supported through SAML, so you'd connect your identity provider and we'd switch off password logins for your whole organization.
And provisioning? When someone leaves, I don't want to rely on a supervisor remembering to remove them from a second system.
SCIM provisioning is in beta right now. We can enable it for you, and deactivating someone in your directory removes their access within a few minutes.
Beta makes me a little nervous, to be honest. What's the fallback if the sync breaks and nobody notices?
Sessions expire every twelve hours, and every login goes through your provider. So even if a sync fails, a removed user can't get back in once their session ends.
And we'd alert your admins if the provisioning sync errors out. I don't think that's in the written answers yet, so let's add it.
Please do. What about shared devices? Some of our crews share one truck tablet between the day and night shifts.
Shared devices work fine. Each person signs in with their own account at shift start, and the app clears cached job data when they sign out.
Good. Moving on, incident notification. If you have a breach involving our data, how quickly do we hear about it?
Our contract commits to notifying you within seventy two hours of discovering an incident. That's on page nine of the master agreement, I believe.
Seventy two hours is tight for us. The commission expects our own report fairly quickly, so whatever time you take eats into our window.
And from a records point of view, I'd need to know which customer records were involved, not just that something happened somewhere.
We'd give you an initial notice first, and then a fuller report with the affected records once the investigation is far enough along.
Okay. Let's park the exact window for a minute. I want to check what the commission guidance actually says before I push back on it.
Related question, while we're on breaches. Who does your penetration testing, and can we see the latest report?
An outside firm tests us every year, application and infrastructure. Ormsby Kade did the last one, and there were no critical findings left open.
Can we get the report itself, or just a summary? Our auditors usually want something with the testing firm's letterhead on it.
We share an executive summary under NDA. The full report stays with us, but you can walk through it with me on a call if needed.
That's normal enough, I'll take the summary. Okay, encryption. I'll read the question: data at rest and in transit, and who holds the keys.
Data at rest is encrypted with AES two fifty six, including backups and photos. In transit, everything is TLS one point two or higher, no exceptions.
Keys live in our cloud provider's key management service. They're rotated every year, and only two people on my team can administer them.
Do you support customer managed keys? A few of the larger vendors we work with have started offering that.
Not today. It's come up a couple of times, but it isn't on the near term roadmap, so I'd rather not promise it.
That's an honest answer, I'll note it as not available. What about the phones? Photos sitting on a technician's phone worry me more than your servers do.
Photos are stored inside the app's encrypted storage, not the camera roll, and they're removed from the phone as soon as they upload.
Speaking of phones, I know your crews asked about offline mode when we did the demo. That's a separate conversation, but it's on its way.
Yes, let's keep that for another day. Next up is data residency, which Beatrix flagged in a few places.
Our policy says customer records can't be stored outside the US. Can you confirm where everything sits, including backups and anyone with support access?
Production runs in our primary US region, and backups replicate to a second US region. Support staff with production access are all US based.
And if a written commitment isn't enough, we could look at a dedicated instance just for Calder, fully separate from our other customers.
A dedicated instance is a much bigger conversation than I expected today. Let me think about whether we actually need that.
Can I go on a quick tangent? Graham, you mentioned the commission audit. Do they publish what they expect from vendors, or is it case by case?
There's a guidance document, about forty pages, mostly common sense. Logging gets the most attention, which brings us neatly to audit logs.
So, what do you log, how long do you keep it, and can we get it out into our own monitoring?
We log sign-ins, failed sign-ins, permission changes, exports, and every edit to a work order, with the before and after values.
Audit logs are kept for one year in the app. You can search them in the admin console and export them as files at any time.
One year won't be enough. The commission looks back over two years, so we'd need at least that, or we'd have to keep copies ourselves.
We can stream the logs to your SIEM, which is how most security teams prefer it anyway. Then your retention rules apply, not ours.
Streaming would be ideal, honestly. What format does it come out in, and is it something you push or something we pull?
We push it, JSON over HTTPS to an endpoint you control, or syslog if your tooling prefers that. Every event has a stable ID, so duplicates are easy to drop.
JSON is fine for us. We'd want to test it well before the audit, though, not in the middle of it.
Then let's set up a test feed with your team. I'll have one running against your endpoint by Friday the twenty third of October.
Also, I need to correct something I said earlier about the pen test. I checked the report folder while we were talking.
Ormsby Kade did our test two years ago. This year's test was done by Larkspire Assurance, finished in May, and that's the summary I'd send you.
Good catch, thanks. Our auditors would have spotted the date on the letterhead straight away. So it's the Larkspire summary we're waiting for.
Yes. I'll send it as soon as your legal team countersigns the NDA. Elena has the document and the latest version.
I sent the NDA over last week, so it's probably sitting with your procurement team. I'll chase it this afternoon.
Back to incident notification. I checked the guidance while Odette was talking. The commission wants our first report inside seventy two hours of us knowing.
So if you take your full seventy two hours, we'd have no time left at all. We'd need something meaningfully shorter than that.

Then I have a second correction, and it's good news. The seventy two hours Elena mentioned is our old template. Our current data processing addendum commits to forty eight hours from when we confirm an incident.
Ah, she's right, I was looking at an older version of the master agreement. Sorry about that, Graham, that one's on me.
No harm done. Forty eight hours from confirmation works for us, as long as the initial notice comes out at that point and the details follow.
And the details should list the affected customer records, like I said earlier. Can that be written into the addendum as well?
Yes, let's write it in: an initial notice within forty eight hours of confirmation, then the list of affected records as soon as we have it.
Can we go back to residency for a moment? I've been thinking about the dedicated instance while you were talking about logs.
Our policy doesn't require separation from other customers. It requires the data to stay in the US, and a contract that says so.
I agree with Beatrix. A dedicated instance means a separate upgrade schedule and more for me to audit every year. I'd rather not.
Then let's drop the dedicated instance. You stay on the shared environment, and we add a residency addendum stating that production data and backups stay in the US.
That's simpler for everyone. I'll ask our counsel to draft the residency addendum alongside the data processing one, so you can review both together.
Perfect. One document review instead of two definitely makes my life easier, and our counsel's too.
There are a few smaller items left, mostly wording. Backup restore testing, vulnerability scanning frequency, and whether you run background checks on staff.
Restores are tested every quarter, we scan continuously, and everyone with production access has a background check before they start. I'll make the wording clearer.
One more, and I have to ask it. We heard about your scheduler outage last month. Was that a security incident?
No, it was a reliability problem, and no data was exposed. There's a public write-up if your auditors want to read about it.
Good enough for me. And on the commission audit, I should correct myself too. They've moved fieldwork up, and it now starts on the eighth of December.
Which means anything we need from you has to be in my hands well before that. The questionnaire especially, with all of today's changes.
Then let me own that. I'll send Beatrix the revised questionnaire, with every correction from today, by Wednesday the fourteenth of October.
The fourteenth is good. Send it to me and copy Graham, and I'll route it to our review committee the same week.
Let me recap so we all leave with the same list. Elena sends the revised questionnaire, and Odette sends the pen test summary and sets up the log feed.
Our counsel drafts the residency and data processing addenda together, and the notification terms go in exactly as we agreed today.
That matches my notes. Thanks, all of you, this was far more useful than another round of email back and forth.
Agreed. And I'll come back to you on the thirty day location history once I've spoken to the union rep.
Perfect, that's everything from us. Thanks Graham, thanks Beatrix, and we'll talk again once the documents are with you.

items.text: Incident notification: initial notice within 48 hours of confirming an incident (the 72 hours first mentioned was the old template), affected records listed afterwards
No dedicated instance for Calder; they stay on the shared environment with a residency addendum keeping production data and backups in the US
Latest penetration test was by Larkspire Assurance (finished in May); Ormsby Kade did the test two years ago
Send Beatrix the revised questionnaire with all of today's corrections by Wednesday October 14
Send the Larkspire executive summary once Calder countersigns the NDA
Set up a test audit-log feed to Calder's SIEM endpoint by Friday October 23
Have counsel draft the residency addendum alongside the data processing addendum
Can location history be shortened to thirty days? Beatrix is checking with the union
